stem: The man ___ lives next door is a doctor.
tests: defining relative pronoun for a person

stem: Look! It ___ now.
tests: present continuous for an action now

stem: I'm interested in ___ Spanish.
You ___ wear a seat belt. It's the law.
Where ___ you go last night?
This is my brother. Do you know ___?
We don't have ___ milk.
tests: any with uncountable noun in a negative

stem: I wish I ___ more free time.
note: Minor: 'wish I would have' is heard in informal US English but is non-standard for a present wish; low risk. Wish + past simple is usually taught at B1-B2.

stem: When we arrived, the film ___ already started.
tests: past perfect for an earlier past event
note: Minor: 'the film was already started' is grammatical as a stative passive and is heard informally, so 'was' is not a fully clean distractor; consider 'did' instead. Past perfect is usually taught at B1.

stem: It was my sister ___ called you.
tests: relative pronoun in an it-cleft (who for a person)
note: The gap is solved by the basic rule who = person (which/what are not standard for a person) without knowing the cleft frame; 'that' is not offered. It effectively measures A2-B1 knowledge, not B2 clefts. Consider testing the frame itself.

stem: I ___ my keys yesterday.
tests: past simple vs present perfect with yesterday

stem: He was very tired. ___, he finished his work.
My car is ___ than yours.
She ___ like coffee.
note: Minor ambiguity: 'She isn't like coffee' is grammatical with 'like' as a preposition (= not similar to), only implausible in meaning. Add context or use a verb that cannot be a preposition (e.g. 'She ___ know the answer').

stem: She can ___ very well.
My parents ___ at home now.
The meeting is ___ Monday.
He isn't answering. He ___ have left already.
Have you ever ___ to London?
I enjoy ___ books in the evening.
We ___ at the cinema yesterday.
She can't talk now. She ___ a shower.
note: Minor: 'has' is grammatical only as habit or possession and is ruled out by 'now'. 'have a shower' is British English (US: take a shower).

stem: I ___ to work yesterday.
If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay at home.
I ___ to the market yesterday.
___ it was raining, we went for a walk.
My brother, ___ lives in Ankara, is a teacher.
tests: relative pronoun in a non-defining clause
note: Minor: 'that' is barred in non-defining clauses by standard grammar and ELT practice, but is heard informally; low risk.

stem: ___ your father speak English?
This house ___ in 1950.
She ___ me that she was tired.
I think she ___ the exam.
I have ___ old car.
tests: a vs an before a vowel sound

stem: If I had known about the party, I ___ last night.
I ___ play football when I was a child.
She denied ___ the money.
This is the ___ restaurant in the city.
I ___ for you for two hours!
My brother ___ in a bank.
My mother is a teacher. ___ works in a school.
I ___ dinner when the phone rang.
tests: past continuous interrupted by past simple

stem: Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later.
The bridge is ___ at the moment.
How ___ money do you need?
She asked me where ___.
tests: reported question: word order and backshift

stem: Look at those clouds. It ___ rain.
I ___ my hair cut yesterday.
We have lived here ___ 2015.
note: Minor: 'from 2015' is non-standard with the present perfect (needs 'since', or 'from 2015 on'), though 'from' is a typical L1 transfer error and so a good distractor; low risk.

stem: If I ___ more money, I would buy a bigger house.
tests: second conditional if-clause (past for unreal present)
note: Minor: 'have' gives 'if + present, would', a mixed pattern heard in informal speech but not a standard second conditional; 'would have' in an if-clause is also non-standard (informal US). Low risk; both rejected.

stem: She ___ know the answer.
tests: present simple negative, 3rd person singular (doesn't + base verb)
note: Sound item. 'don't' is heard in some dialects and song lyrics ('She don't know') but is non-standard, so it is a fair distractor; 'isn't' is a plain be + bare verb error. Solvable by subject-verb agreement alone, which is the target.

stem: I ___ to school yesterday.
tests: past simple of an irregular verb (go -> went) with a past time marker
note: Sound item. 'yesterday' rules out 'go'. 'goed' is a non-word (over-regularisation), so it can be rejected on sight without applying any rule; fine as an A1 distractor but it checks word recognition more than grammar. Same in British and American English.

stem: She can't talk now. She ___ dinner.
tests: present continuous for an action in progress now (dynamic 'have' = eat a meal) vs present simple
note: Only 'is having' is listed. 'has' is the option to watch: 'She has dinner' is well-formed as a habitual or scheduled reading and the stem has no time phrase to block it. After 'She can't talk now.' a bare simple present for an action in progress reads as a learner error, so I rate it unacceptable, but a pedant could defend it. To close the gap add a present-moment cue, e.g. 'She ___ dinner right now.' 'have' fails on agreement, so the item is effectively a two-way choice.

stem: When we arrived, the film ___ already started.
tests: past perfect simple for an event before a past reference point (when + past simple)
note: 'did' fails: 'did already started' is ungrammatical (the emphatic 'did already start' reading is blocked by the past form 'started'). 'has' fails: present perfect cannot go with the past-time clause 'When we arrived'. Both are eliminable by form or time marker. Easy for B2: past perfect simple after 'when' is usually taught at B1; consider labelling it B1 or testing a B2 use (past perfect continuous, 'by the time', reported speech, third conditional).

stem: ___ I need is a long holiday.
note: Only 'What' works: 'That I need is ...' has no complete clause or free relative (needs 'All that I need is ...' or archaic 'That which I need ...'), and 'Which I need is ...' has no set of alternatives to choose from. Easy for B2: 'What I need is ...' is a very common chunk, so it can be solved without analysing the structure. Dialect: 'holiday' is British; American English usually says 'vacation' (though 'holiday' is understood).
